newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Prague bourse decline nearing end, analysts say.
newsitem.headline: Prague bourse decline nearing end, analysts say.

text.p: The Prague Stock Exchange, hit hard recently by problems in the banking sector and poor economic indicators, is nearing the end of its downturn as fundamentals begin to lure investors back, analysts said.
The PSE has lost just over five percent in the last week, after the failure of Kreditni Banka led to the fifth biggest Czech bank, Agrobanka, being put under forced administration.

The banking crisis also brought about a wave of speculation that senior Czech officials, including Finance Minister Ivan Kocarnik and central bank Governor Josef Tosovsky may be forced to resign in the wake of political battles it caused.
But a surge in blue chips on Thursday pushed the bourse up for the first time in eight sessions, giving rise to optimism among traders that the market would now show signs of recovery.
The PX50 index closed on Thursday at 548.9, up 2.5 points.
"The decline was really not based on fundamental changes, but events related to Agrobanka and speculation about Kocarnik and Tosovsky," Daniel Gladis of Atlantik Financni Trhy told Reuters.
Ivan Kusacek of Zivnostenska Banka added: "I expect the market should stabilise by the end of the week, and investor interest could increase by next week."

On September 17, the Czech National Bank placed Agrobanka under forced administration after it suffered liquidity problems due to Kreditni's failure and the investigation of people in the case who are also connected to Agrobanka.

But Gladis said the move is another badly-needed step in reforming the banking sector -- the CNB has now placed 12 banks under some form of supervision over the past two years, shutting many -- and should speed up overall market reforms.
"I think that people will realise that what happened is actually a positive sign for the market because it is forcing a cleanup," he added.

The Czech capital market has long been cast by investors as being murky, where little regulation and poor enforcement of laws allow most trading to be done off-market with only a trickle of information being made public.

They point to Agrobanka's problems, which are considered to stem from its dealings with Motoinvest, an investment group shrouded in secrecy that stormed onto the market last year with a series of takeover battles against big institutions.

One official from Motoinvest was indicted on criminal fraud charges for a debt swap scheme which police said led, in part, to Kreditni's failure with losses of nearly 12 billion czech crowns ($445.1 million).

Agrobanka is the largest wholly-private Czech bank with basic capital of some four billion crowns at the end of last year. Motoinvest has denied any responsibility for any of the problems at Kreditni or Agrobanka, where people associated with the group hold board seats.

Adding to the market's woes have been some unfavourable economic figures in the last week, such as a slight slowdown in GDP growth to 4.0 percent in the second quarter from 4.6 in the first quarter, and January-August trade figures showing an all-time record deficit of 100.9 billion crowns.
"The Czech Republic has usually had good macro-economic numbers, but some of the more recent figures are not so rosy," said Jay King of Wood and Company.
"With these weaknesses and the bourse's good run before that, there has been a nice chance to take profits. I'm not sure if we will see the investors return so quickly to boost the market."
